scenario.title: A variety with no route to change
scenario.intro: A maize team in Kenya is writing a concept note. They know their science: two agro-ecologies, a drought-tolerant candidate ready for release, a seed company willing to multiply it. What they have never written is a results chain. The note says the variety will be released and incomes will rise, and nothing about what has to happen in between. The MEAL review is in ten days. This module gives you the chain, the assumptions on each link and the roles, so the note can say how a release becomes a change for farmers.

objectives.text: Trace a project's activities through processes, outputs, outcomes and impact and explain why no level is proof of the next.
State the assumption behind each link in a results chain and name the evidence that would test it.
Distinguish the adoption pathways the MEAL Matrix describes for seed systems, digital advice and upstream science, and match a project to its pathway.
Explain when in the lifecycle the theory of change is co-developed and which role is accountable and which responsible for it.
Draft a results chain for a proposal at concept-note stage, with assumptions on each link and impact stated as a contribution.

lessons.title: What a theory of change does for a proposal

beats.hook: The concept note says the variety will be released and incomes will rise. A reviewer asks one question: how? The theory of change is the written answer.

example.title: The concept note as it arrived
body: Three pages. Breeding objectives for two agro-ecologies. A list of trial sites. A release target for year two. A seed company partnership mentioned in one line. Then a final sentence: the variety will raise maize yields and household incomes in the target counties.

Section 5.1 asks the project, in Phase 1, to define its intended results, intervention logic, investor requirements, geography, target populations and operational feasibility. The note has geography and intended results. It has no intervention logic. Nobody has written down the steps between release and income.

The theory of change is where that logic goes. Central MEAL co-develops it with the team at concept and proposal design. It traces the project's activities through outputs and outcomes to impact: trials run, variety released, seed sold, farmers plant it, gains that last. Each step is a different kind of result and will need its own evidence.

The chain then feeds the Phase 1 gate: a MEAL section, a KPI crosswalk, an indicative data architecture and a costed MEAL budget, all before submission. Without the chain, the team cannot pick KPIs or cost the evidence, because it does not yet know what has to change.
The rule behind the timing is simple. MEAL must enter before indicators, budgets and data systems are fixed. A chain written after the award inherits whatever the budget allowed.

bullets: The theory of change is the project's intervention logic written as a results chain: processes, outputs, outcomes, impact.
It is co-developed with central MEAL in Phase 1, opportunity and proposal, before indicators, budgets and data systems are fixed.
It feeds the Phase 1 gate: MEAL section, KPI crosswalk, indicative data architecture and costed MEAL budget before submission.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

lessons.title: Building the chain: processes, outputs, outcomes, impact

beats.hook: Four slabs connect left to right. The slabs are easy to write. The links between them are where a proposal quietly promises more than it can show.

example.title: The maize chain, slab by slab
body: Processes. Trials run with national partners in two agro-ecologies. Two seed companies engaged. Workplan and budget tracked. Evidence: workplans, financial records, the partnership registry. This is what the team does.

Outputs. The variety released and registered. Certified seed produced and sold by the companies. Field days held in the target counties. Evidence: delivery records, trial results, training logs, distribution systems. This is what the team delivers.

Outcomes. Farmers plant the variety on their own plots. The seed companies keep multiplying it on their own account. Evidence: adoption surveys, partner records. This is what changes for people and partners. Section 2.3 calls it the level where CIMMYT's contribution becomes most visible.

Impact. Yield and income gains that last, interpreted alongside rainfall, prices and other actors. Evidence: panels, impact evaluations, remote sensing, external data. Section 2.4 is explicit: CIMMYT does not claim to be the sole cause. The chain states a contribution.

The logic is cumulative, but no slab proves the next. Section 2 says different types of data serve different analytical purposes and do not all carry the same evidential weight. Field days held does not show farmers planted. Farmers planted does not show gains lasted.

bullets: Processes are what you do, outputs what you deliver, outcomes what changes for people and partners, impact what lasts in agrifood systems.
The logic is cumulative, but each level needs its own evidence; delivery is the foundation for outcome evidence, not a substitute for it.
The impact link is a contribution alongside other factors, never a claim to be the sole cause.

source.title: The MEAL Framework: From Data to Impact

lessons.title: Assumptions: the links you cannot control

beats.hook: Seed is sold. Do farmers plant it? That depends on things the project does not control. Every link in your chain hides one of these. The job is to write them down.

example.title: Three tags for the maize chain
body: Link one, processes to outputs. Trials run, so the variety is released. Assumption: the national release process accepts the candidate on the trial evidence, and the seed companies produce certified seed in time for the season. Evidence that would test it: release records and the seed registry. Both are operational records the project already keeps.

Link two, outputs to outcomes. Seed is sold and field days held, so farmers plant the variety. Assumption: seed reaches the agro-dealers farmers actually use, at a price they will pay, and farmers choose it over what they planted last year. Evidence: an adoption survey among farmers who bought seed or attended a field day, with persistent identifiers so the two records link.

Link three, outcomes to impact. Farmers plant it, so yields and incomes rise and stay up. Assumption: the gain holds across seasons and markets, not only in a good year. Evidence: panel data interpreted alongside rainfall and price series, which section 2.6 lists as context data needed to interpret change.

The MEAL Matrix names this check for every project type. Seed systems: check that the adoption and diffusion logic holds. Applied agronomy: check that field monitoring is consistent with expected outcomes and adoption logic. System change: check the project's contribution to systemic outcomes and the assumptions in its theory of change. Breeding and upstream science: periodic review against the theory of change.
An assumption with no planned evidence is a hope. Once it is written down with its evidence, it becomes a row in the measurement plan and a learning question for the quarterly review.

bullets: At each link ask: what has to be true, outside the project's control, for the next level to happen?
Write the assumption down and pair it with the data source that could show it failing.
The Matrix asks seed projects to check their adoption and diffusion logic and system change projects to check the assumptions in their theory of change.

lessons.title: Three pathways compared: seed systems, digital advice, upstream science

beats.hook: Three concept notes all promise adoption. One sells seed, one sends advice to phones, one edits a gene. The route from output to outcome is different in each. Copy the wrong one and the chain breaks.

example.title: Which pathway does the Matrix describe?
example.prompt: Each statement comes from one row of the MEAL Matrix. Drop it on the project type whose theory of change it belongs to.

bins.label: Upstream discovery science
bins.hint: Scientific advances, innovation readiness, impact pathways.

cards.label: Check that the adoption and diffusion logic holds
cards.why: The seed systems row asks MEAL to check that the adoption and diffusion logic holds beyond distribution records.

cards.label: Seed registry and distribution data are what the project contributes
cards.why: Seed pilots contribute operational output reporting and seed registry and distribution data.

cards.label: Track adoption and varietal diffusion at regional scale through digital registries
cards.why: At Medium scale the seed systems row sets up digital registries and adoption dashboards to track diffusion regionally.

cards.label: A user-centred theory of change covering usefulness, behaviour change and relevance
cards.why: This is the Small column of the digital agriculture and AI row.

cards.label: Usage, engagement and analytics KPIs
cards.why: Digital pilots define usage, engagement and analytics KPIs so the path from advice to practice can be followed.

cards.label: Link advisory effectiveness to adoption pathways and behaviour change
cards.why: At Medium scale the digital row links advisory effectiveness to adoption pathways and behaviour change.

cards.label: Connect scientific advances to impact pathways and innovation readiness
cards.why: The Medium column of the upstream discovery science row connects advances to impact pathways and innovation readiness.

cards.label: Periodic review of laboratory outputs against the theory of change
cards.why: Small upstream projects get a results framework and periodic review against their theory of change.

cards.label: Research data and laboratory output monitoring are what the project contributes
cards.why: Upstream projects contribute operational monitoring of laboratory outputs and research data for reporting.

bullets: Seed systems: seed multiplied and distributed, farmers adopt, the variety diffuses; MEAL checks that the adoption and diffusion logic holds.
Digital advice: advice is useful and users engage before practice changes; the theory of change covers usefulness, behaviour change and relevance.
Upstream science: scientific advances connect to impact pathways and innovation readiness; a laboratory output is not farmer adoption.

lessons.title: Ownership: who holds which part of the chain

beats.hook: The Regional MEAL Lead drafted the chain. So is it MEAL's document now? The RACI matrix says no, and the difference matters when the chain has to be defended.

example.title: One row, four roles
body: The RACI row reads: develop the theory of change and results framework. Project lead: A. Regional MEAL Lead: R. Design, Standards and Enablement pillar: C. Evaluation, Learning and Accountability pillar: C. One A per activity.

Accountable means the project lead owns the result. If a reviewer asks why the chain skips an outcome, it is the project lead who answers. Responsible means the Regional MEAL Lead does the work: facilitates the session, drafts the slabs and links, checks the pathway against the Matrix row. Holding the pen does not transfer ownership.

The two pillars are consulted. The Design pillar leads theory of change and results architecture work for complex or strategic proposals and approves results architectures; its stated purpose is to stop weak theories of change being locked in at proposal stage. The Evaluation pillar is consulted because the chain will shape the learning and evaluation questions it later owns.

Scale changes the intensity, not the row. For a Small project that proceeds with the standard package, the Regional MEAL Lead's Phase 1 role is limited to confirming the classification and the base budget. Large and MEGA projects co-design MEAL with the team from the start of proposal development.

After submission the chain stays live. Phase 2 confirms the results chain at inception. Phase 5 uses quarterly or seasonal reviews to adapt. Phase 6 applies contribution analysis to it. The Project MEAL Focal Point, appointed in Phase 2, maintains the MEAL plan built on it.

bullets: Project lead accountable, Regional MEAL Lead responsible, Design and Evaluation pillars consulted: one A per activity.
For Small projects on the standard package, the Regional MEAL Lead's Phase 1 role is limited to confirming the classification and the base budget.
The chain is confirmed at inception and revisited in reviews and contribution analysis; ownership does not end at submission.

lessons.title: Worked example: draft a chain for a maize variety project in 6 minutes

beats.hook: Ten days to the MEAL review. The team has the science and no chain. Here is how to get a reviewable draft on one page before the budget is fixed.

example.title: Put the maize chain in order
example.prompt: The team's six steps are scrambled. Arrange them from the first process to the lasting change. Think: what is done, what is delivered, what changes, what lasts.

items.label: Trials run with national partners; two seed companies engaged
items.detail: Process: the activities and partnerships that enable delivery.

items.label: Certified seed sold by the companies; field days held in target counties
items.detail: Output: services and seed delivered. Assumption on the next link: seed reaches dealers farmers use.

items.label: Farmers plant the variety on their own plots
items.detail: Outcome: a change in practice among beneficiaries.

items.label: Seed companies keep multiplying the variety on their own account in later seasons
items.detail: Outcome: a partner's behaviour and business system changed, sustained by farmer demand.

items.label: Lasting yield and income gains among adopters, as a contribution alongside other factors
items.detail: Impact: positive, lasting change, stated as a contribution.

example.why: The chain runs process, output, output, outcome, outcome, impact. Trials come first because nothing can be released without them. Release precedes seed sales and field days. Farmers planting comes before the companies' independent multiplication, because the proposal's logic is that demand shown in the first seasons is what keeps the companies producing. Impact is last and is written as a contribution, not a sole-cause claim.

bullets: Six moves: four slabs, a tag on every link, evidence for each tag, impact as a contribution, one learning question, a pathway check against your Matrix row.
The chain is element one of the minimum package, results architecture, together with decision and learning questions and links to CIMMYT Strategy.
Draft it at concept-note stage, before indicators, budgets and data systems are fixed.

storyboards.title: Building the chain: four slabs, three links

frames.narration: A results chain is four slabs and three links. The slabs are easy. The links are where proposals go wrong.
Slab one: processes. Trials run with national partners. Slab two: outputs. A variety released, seed sold, field days held. Slab three: outcomes. Farmers plant it. Slab four: impact. Gains that last.

frames.narration: Now hang a tag on each link. Each tag is an assumption: something the chain relies on but the project does not control. Write them down. A link without a tag is a hope, not a plan.

links.label: Assumes: release approved; seed ready for the season
Assumes: seed reaches dealers; farmers choose it
Assumes: gains hold across seasons and markets

frames.narration: Follow one farmer along the chain. She attends a field day. That is an output. She plants the variety next season. That is an outcome. Nothing at slab two told you slab three would happen.
Now the assumption fails. Certified seed never reaches her agro-dealer. Outputs are complete. The outcome slab stays empty. The chain breaks at the link, not at the slab.
The last link is different again. Impact is lasting change. CIMMYT does not claim to be the sole cause. The chain states a contribution alongside rainfall, prices and other actors.
Slabs are what you deliver and what changes. Links are what you assume. Name each one and plan the evidence that will test it.

frames.narration: Three project types, three different routes from output to outcome. The Matrix describes each one. Copying the wrong route is a common proposal error.
Seed systems: seed is multiplied and distributed, farmers adopt it, and the variety diffuses. MEAL checks that the adoption and diffusion logic holds, with registries and adoption dashboards.

Digital advice: the chain runs through usefulness and engagement before practice changes. The Matrix asks for a user-centred theory of change covering usefulness, behaviour change and relevance, with usage and engagement KPIs.
Upstream science: the chain connects scientific advances to impact pathways and innovation readiness. It does not pretend that a laboratory output is farmer adoption.

Match the logic to the type. Adoption and diffusion belongs to seed systems. Usefulness and engagement to digital. Innovation readiness to upstream science. Seed logic dropped into a digital project bounces back.
